segments.say: Seven agents, an hour of work, two thousand three hundred lines of source - and how many commits. One. Then two once the CI workflow landed, and three after the pull request merged. All of the building is inside the first one. Read the log bottom to top. Signal desk v one, then ci: run the suite on every push and pull request, then the alerts buffer trim that came in as pull request two. Two of the three are housekeeping. The product itself - simulator, rules engine, server, two client panels, the shell that holds them - is one line of that log. And that is not the number I would have predicted from watching it.

And that is not a tidiness complaint, so let us make it concrete: what does it cost, in commands that do not work. Notice the shape of the ask, because it is what makes the answer usable. Name the commands that would work if each task had committed separately, and for each one say what question it would have answered. A cost you can name a command for is a cost you can argue about. Git log on a file tells you nothing, because every file arrived at the same instant. Git blame attributes two thousand three hundred lines to one commit made by me, which is false about all of it. Git bisect has nothing to search - there is one revision, and it either has the bug or it does not. And git show, on the commit that introduced a behaviour, shows you the entire product. Every one of those is a question you will want to ask in three weeks and will not be able to. And I told it how the commit happened - seven tasks, untracked files, one commit by me at the end. Without that it would have answered about git in general instead of this repository. There is one more that hurts and only shows up later: you cannot revert a piece of it. If the rules engine turns out to be wrong in a way that is not worth fixing, the only revert available takes the whole product with it.

And it is worth being clear about why it happened, because it was not carelessness. The orchestrator does not commit. It writes files. The commit was mine, at the end, once everything was on disk - which is the obvious thing to do and it is what anybody would have done. And it puts real numbers on the squash. Thirty-eight files, four thousand one hundred and twenty-three insertions, one author timestamp. Seven tasks with a real dependency graph - simulator first, then the rules engine, two client panels running in parallel, then the server, then the shell, then a verification pass that needs all of it. All that structure existed while the build ran. None of it survives in the history. The history is not missing because somebody forgot. It is missing because nothing in the design ever created it. And this is the shape of most defects in a pipeline like this one, which is worth naming. Not a bug. An absence.

So: the smallest change that would have prevented it. Seven commands on screen, each with the question it would have answered underneath it. Bisect: which task's commit introduced the regression. Blame: which brief governs this line. Log with a time range: did the scheduler really run the two client tasks in parallel, and what did each one cost. Every one is answerable in a normal repository and unanswerable in this one. And it ends with a line worth stealing. It did not try to work out which task wrote which line, because that is not recoverable from git - no per-task branches, nothing in the task list beyond a file list - so any claim about it would be a guess and not evidence. And the interesting part is where it belongs. You could tell each task to commit its own work, in its brief - and then a task that fails halfway commits half of itself, and a task that touches a file it does not own commits somebody else's change along with it. The runner already knows when a task started, when it finished, and whether it succeeded. It is the only thing in the system that knows all three. So the commit belongs there: after a task reports done, stage what changed and commit it in that task's name. And notice that the argument for putting it in the runner is the same argument that put the tool grant there. Anything that has to be true across all tasks, regardless of what any individual task is doing, belongs to the thing that runs them. Anything specific to one job belongs in that job's brief.

And look at what that one change buys, because it is more than a tidy log. About twenty lines of diff and one new import. That is the whole change - a helper that stages exactly the files the task declared, filtered to the ones that actually exist on disk, and commits them under the task's id and area. Never git add dash A, so a task that wrote outside its declared files, or a failed task's leftovers, never rides along in a commit that is not its own. Seven commits instead of one means you can revert the rules engine and keep everything else. It means the diff for any single area is one command away. It means the next time a build like this goes wrong at task five, you can look at exactly what task five did without reading the other six. That is the difference between a generated pile you have to accept or discard whole, and generated work you can take apart. It runs synchronously, on purpose, so that with three tasks in flight no two sets of git commands can interleave. It also changes what a failed run leaves behind. Today, a build that dies at task five leaves a working tree with four tasks' worth of unattributed changes in it and nothing to tell you which is which.

There is a general version of this worth carrying out of the week. Anything that produces a lot of work quickly should produce a lot of history quickly, and it almost never does by default - because writing files is the job and recording what happened is somebody's afterthought. The diff is on screen and most of it is comment. Seven lines of prose explaining why the commit runs synchronously and why it never stages anything the task did not declare, sitting above six lines that do the work. That ratio is deliberate in code you expect an agent to read months from now. If you build a pipeline like this one, put the record in before you need it. You will only want it on the day it is too late to add. A record has to be written by the thing doing the work, at the moment it does it. Reconstructed afterwards, it is a story. And it is the same argument as the log, one level down. The log records that something happened. The history records what it did.

And now the sentence that should have been there this morning. The memory file says zero dependencies. The orchestrator needs one. I knew that, I said it out loud in the lecture where we installed it, and I did not write it down - so an agent reading only what was written deleted the dependency, exactly as instructed, and left the program that built this repository unable to run. Read the phrasing in the prompt, because it decides what comes back. The rule was incomplete, not wrong. It is what stops the fix from being: delete the rule. Then three things it has to record: which file needs the package, why that file is a development tool rather than part of the shipped app, and what stays true regardless - the console still starts with no network and nothing beyond Node. The third is the one people leave out, and it is the one that keeps a rule a rule. It is a small, specific, entirely avoidable failure, and I am spending a lecture on it because the general form is the most expensive thing in this whole way of working. Not a model doing something strange.

So read what it wrote, because it is better than what I would have written. It does the install first, and part of what it does was not in my instruction. It puts the package under devDependencies rather than dependencies, because only the build tool needs it. Then it checks that gitignore still excludes node modules, and runs npm start and npm test to confirm both still work with no network involvement - the actual claim the rule makes, tested rather than assumed. The folder appears in the sidebar, the lock file arrives untracked, and nothing that ships changed. It names the file. It says why that file is different: a development tool invoked by a person from the command line, not code the running app loads or serves. It states the boundary - nothing under server, nothing under public, and nothing npm start reaches may import from it. And then a clause I did not ask for and would not have thought to add: this does not reopen the door in general, and a new development dependency needs the same justification this one has, not that it was convenient. Read that against what I actually said out loud when we installed it, which was roughly: this is a deliberate exception, it is a tool not the app. Every one of those clauses is in there, plus three I did not say, plus the boundary written as a rule instead of an intention.

That is what a written standard looks like when it is actually finished. Not a rule. A rule, its exception, the reason for the exception, and the reason the exception does not generalise. Most of the rules in most repositories are the first quarter of that, which is why they get broken by reasonable people doing reasonable things. The orchestrator diff is back on screen, and the two changes are one kind of change. One adds a commit per task, so the history records what happened. The other adds an exception, so the rule records what is allowed. Neither is a feature. Both are the repository learning to say true things about itself. And the entire cost of not having it here was one deleted package and one tool that stopped working, on a day when somebody happened to be watching. On a day when nobody is, it is a rule everybody quietly ignores, which is worse, because then you do not have a standard - you have a document. There is a practical version of this you can apply on Monday, and it takes about a minute. Whenever you find yourself saying out loud that something is an exception, stop and write it into the file that states the rule. Not later, not in the pull request, not in a comment on the line - in the document that the next agent, and the next person, will actually read. Look at what changed in the old paragraph, because it is one phrase. Nothing in dependencies or devDependencies became nothing in dependencies. That is the rule narrowing by exactly the width of the exception, no wider - and then the exception gets its own paragraph underneath, naming the file. One phrase out, one paragraph in. Npm start and npm test never import it, and neither reaches the network. The test for whether you have finished is simple: if the only place the exception exists is in your memory of having said it, you have not written a standard.
